Hi Sara — thanks again for the call earlier. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we stay aligned: 

Key takeaways:
- FinPay priorities: predictable unit cost, sub-200ms p95 for short completions, customer data residency, and SSO/KMS requirements.
- You want a head-to-head cost/TCO comparison vs hyperscalers and a small set of production-like tests to validate latency and unit economics.

Proposed next tests (able to run this week):
1) 1M-token streamed generation run (real prompt mix) — measure tokens/sec, p50/p95, and per-1M effective cost.
2) Batching matrix: single-request, batch=4, batch=8 — measure cost delta and tail latency impact.
3) Cache-hit simulation: run 10k repeating prefixes to estimate effective cache hit rate and token savings.
4) Failure/fallback exercise: route to cheaper capacity variant when load spikes to observe graceful degradation.

What we'll deliver:
- Redwood-hosted per-1M token estimate (with assumptions) + modeled TCO in spreadsheet.
- Raw benchmark CSV with latency and throughput.
- Suggested canary test plan and config for Dedicated lanes if you want an apples-to-apples dedicated run.

Ask from your side:
- Confirm the prompt mix (we can use the post-call sample you uploaded or you can share a representative 1k prompt set).
- Any strict SLA targets besides the p95 target above?
- Who from procurement should I loop in for preliminary pricing/terms?

Attaching: canary_test_plan.md (stub) — basic plan and required artifacts.

Thanks — I’ll follow up with a baseline per-1M token estimate shortly so you can budget the tests.

Best,
Aditya Rao
Enterprise Sales

Subject: RE: Recap: Competitive TCO follow-up & next tests (FinPay)

Sara — appreciate the prompt details. Based on the prompt mix you described and our recent benchmark runs, here are baseline unit economics and assumptions (high-level):

Assumptions (used in spreadsheet):
- Token definition: 3.5 chars ~= 1 token (standard).
- Mix: short=60% (avg 90 tokens), mid=30% (avg 320 tokens), long=10% (avg 900 tokens).
- Cache hit: modeled at 25% baseline; we’ll run curves at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%.
- Batching: effective batching saves kernel overhead — modeled improvements measured at batch=4 (~12% token-cost reduction), batch=8 (~20% reduction) for this model family.
- Throughput/latency measured on A100/mixed-precision quantized variant for apples-to-apples; we can run Dedicated variants as requested.

Baseline per-1M token effective cost (hosted):
- Redwood Hosted (with caching & batching assumptions above): ~$22 per 1M input+output tokens
- AWS managed inference baseline (hyperscaler reference): ~$38–42 per 1M tokens (depends on instance type & batching)
- GCP/Vertex reference: ~$40 per 1M tokens

Notes on numbers:
- These are modeled estimates for a like-for-like capability (same model size/quantization). Hyperscaler numbers include instance amortization + inference runtime overhead. Redwood’s advantage here is optimized runtime, KV/prefix caching, and autoscaling efficiency which reduce per-token marginal cost.
- Batching and cache hit rate are the biggest levers. Example: at 50% cache hit and batch=8, effective cost for your mix drops ~35% vs the non-batched, no-cache baseline.

Attached: redwood_cost_model_v1.xlsx (cost breakdown + sensitivity tabs) and finpay_model_benchmarks.csv (raw latency/throughput data from a couple of runs). Will upload EU-region runs if you need EU-only.

Next steps:
- We can schedule a 30-minute session with Marcus (our solutions lead) to walk the spreadsheet and define the exact canary run config.
- If procurement wants an indicative quote (with discount bands for committed volume), we can produce a draft term sheet once we have target monthly token volumes.

I’ll also include a short note on data residency options and KMS flow in a follow-up email.

Best,
Aditya
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
